title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
data_curation: Not a focus of this paper. Training uses rule-based Math-Verify outcome rewards (R=1 if the response contains the correct final answer, else 0); the minimalist recipe trains on MATH level 3-5 questions, a template x coverage study compares ORZ-57k, MATH-12k, GSM-8K, and ASDiv-2K question sets, and the Llama continual-pretraining arm uses the FineMath dataset plus a concatenated corpus built from NuminaMath-1.5 (2 epochs, lr 1e-5).
curriculum: The paper studies the R1-Zero-like paradigm: RL applied directly to a base model with no SFT, no KL term (beta=0), and a rule-based verifier reward. The main recipe is Qwen2.5-Math-7B + Qwen-Math template -> Dr. GRPO RL on MATH level 3-5 (~27h on 8xA100). For weak base models (Llama-3.2-3B) they insert a continual math-pretraining stage (FineMath, then concatenated NuminaQA) before RL to raise the RL ceiling. A template-by-question-set study shows RL can reconstruct capability destroyed by template mismatch and that even small out-of-distribution sets (GSM-8K) can induce reasoning when the template matches. Multi-stage curriculum ordering itself is not the primary focus.
method: Core contribution is Dr. GRPO (GRPO Done Right). Standard GRPO sets per-token advantage A_i,t = (R(q,o_i) - mean(R)) / std(R) and averages the PPO-clipped surrogate over |o_i| tokens. The authors identify two biases: (1) response-level length bias from dividing by |o_i| - for correct (positive-advantage) responses shorter answers get larger gradients, while for incorrect (negative) ones longer answers are penalized less, artificially inflating incorrect-response length; (2) question-level difficulty bias from dividing by std(R), which up-weights near-trivial/near-impossible questions. Dr. GRPO simply removes both the |o_i| length normalization and the std(R) normalization, recovering the PPO objective with Monte-Carlo return and an unbiased group-mean baseline (equivalent to REINFORCE-Leave-One-Out up to a learning-rate-absorbable scale). They also fix biased open-source PPO loss implementations (trl, verl, OpenRLHF, SimpleRL-Zero, Open-Reasoner-Zero) that normalize by response length, replacing mask.sum with the constant generation budget. KL is dropped (beta=0) since rule-based verifiers avoid distributional-shift concerns, saving the reference-model memory/compute. Reward is a sparse 1/0 outcome verifier (Math-Verify), implemented in the Oat framework with actor-learner collocation.
eval_metrics: Benchmarks: AIME 2024, AMC, MATH500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, evaluated with greedy decoding and a 3k-token budget (8k for longer-context baselines). Metrics: accuracy (averaged over 5 benchmarks), pass@8 for exploration, response/token length for efficiency, training reward, plus GPT-4o-mini judging for answering-rate and self-reflection ('Aha moment') detection via keyword+LLM cross-validation. Headline: Oat-Zero-7B (Qwen2.5-Math-7B + Dr. GRPO) reaches 43.3% AIME 2024 and 51.4% average - a new SOTA for 7B R1-Zero-like training, beating SimpleRL-Zero-7B (26.7/46.6), PRIME-Zero-7B (16.7/48.0), OpenReasoner-Zero-7B@8k (13.3/45.9), and R1-Distill-Qwen-7B@3k (10.0/28.5), in 27h on 8xA100. Oat-Zero-1.5B averages 42.1; Oat-Zero-3B (Llama-3.2-3B-NuminaQA) averages 14.8. Dr. GRPO substantially shortens incorrect-response length versus vanilla GRPO with matched-or-better accuracy, confirmed significant across 3 random seeds.
key_results: Oat-Zero-7B (Qwen2.5-Math-7B + Dr. GRPO on MATH L3-5) achieves 43.3% on AIME 2024 and 51.4% average over 5 math benchmarks, a new SOTA for 7B R1-Zero-like training, in 27h on 8xA100. Dr. GRPO cuts incorrect-response length versus vanilla GRPO while matching or improving accuracy (significant over 3 seeds).
evolution_note: Builds on DeepSeek-R1-Zero's (2025) RL-without-SFT paradigm and DeepSeekMath's GRPO (2024), and reacts critically to the 'Aha moment'/long-CoT emergence narrative by showing that both pretraining biases in base models and GRPO's length/difficulty biases inflate response length. Dr. GRPO's removal of length and std normalization prefigured later RLVR correctives (e.g., DAPO-style decoupled clipping and overlong filtering) and motivated closer scrutiny of base-model pretraining biases in R1-Zero replications.
